slides.text: The women of Chhattisgarh were present at every moment of Gandhi's two visits — giving gold at Machilabad in 1920, standing before bayonets at Tamora in 1930, cooking for Gandhi at Devri in 1933, washing his feet in Raipur. Half the movement, half the story, told fully now.
slides.visualDescription: Title card: A collage of the women of the Chhattisgarh freedom movement — the Machilabad donors of 1920, Dayavati before the rifle in 1930, the Devri cooks of 1933, the Raipur elder washing Gandhi's feet. Their faces as the series' other half. Long overdue.

slides.text: December 20, 1920. The women's gathering at Machilabad, Tatyapara, Raipur. A large number of Muslim women attended openly — which was itself an act of courage in 1920. They donated to the Tilak Fund. Hindu and Muslim women on the same ground, for the same cause.
slides.visualDescription: The Machilabad women's gathering, December 1920 — Muslim women who had rarely attended public events, Hindu women from the same neighbourhood, side by side. Their donation to the Tilak Fund. The gold rings and silver bangles. The public act of two communities giving together.

slides.text: Their gold rings and silver bangles went into the Tilak Swaraj Fund. Personal jewelry — the most intimate form of wealth for women in this era — given publicly, to a political cause. The political and the personal fused in the act of giving. The most complete form of commitment.
slides.visualDescription: The gold rings and silver bangles in the Tilak Fund bag — close-up. Each piece of jewelry: a woman's decision to give something personal for something collective. The intimacy of the sacrifice. The most personal wealth given for the most public cause.

slides.text: These women are not named in the historical record. The men who received the fund are named — Gandhi, the collectors, the Congress leaders. The women who gave: unnamed. History's asymmetry: it records the hands that received and forgets the hands that gave.
slides.visualDescription: The historical asymmetry made visible — the names of the men in the record: Gandhi, Shukla, Srivastava. The women of Machilabad: unnamed. The contrast between the recorded and the unrecorded. The fund growing from unnamed hands. History's debt to the unnamed.

slides.text: The Muslim women of Machilabad who attended openly in 1920 — their presence itself an act of social courage. Women's public participation in political gatherings was not the norm. They were there anyway. The movement beginning by exceeding the norms that defined it.
slides.visualDescription: Muslim women at the Machilabad gathering — their presence transgressing the social norms of purdah and women's public participation in 1920. Their being there: as courageous as the donation. The movement expanding what was possible by insisting on the possible.

slides.text: The Hindu-Muslim unity of the 1920 women's gathering — Muslim and Hindu women donating together, on the same ground, to the same cause — was a political statement as significant as any resolution passed at the Nagpur Congress session.
slides.visualDescription: The unity of the Machilabad gathering — Hindu and Muslim women side by side. The political statement: India's women, across the religious line that would eventually partition the country, together in December 1920. The alternative India visible in a women's gathering.

slides.text: The 1920 Kankalipara meeting also had women present. After the meeting, people took bricks from the stage. Among those who took bricks: women. Their hands in the brick-taking. Their homes where the bricks were kept. The movement preserved in women's domestic spaces.
slides.visualDescription: Women at the Kankalipara stage, December 1920 — taking bricks with the same reverence as the men. Their hands on the same bricks. Carrying them home. Placing them on family altars. The movement preserved in the domestic space that women maintained. The home as archive.

slides.text: 1921. The Non-Cooperation Movement spreading through Chhattisgarh. Women boycotting foreign goods — not as secondary participants following their husbands but as primary actors making their own choice. The boycott required someone to manage the household without foreign cloth. Women managed.
slides.visualDescription: Women managing the household boycott of foreign cloth in 1921 — weaving khadi, spinning on the charkha, managing the family economy without imported goods. The domestic economy as the front line of the boycott. Women as the boycott's essential practitioners.

slides.text: The charkha in women's hands. Gandhi's insistence on the charkha as the symbol of self-reliance was not abstract for the women of Chhattisgarh — they had always spun. What Gandhi made political, women had always practised. The charkha: women's tool, then national symbol.
slides.visualDescription: The charkha in women's hands — spinning that had always been women's work, now elevated to national symbol. The women of Chhattisgarh who had spun for generations before Gandhi made it political. Their skill predating the symbol. Their hands the original argument.

slides.text: 1930. The Tamora Jungle Satyagraha. Women in the front lines. Not as supporters but as Satyagrahis. Standing before police bayonets. Being beaten. Not retaliating. The women of Tamora practising the method with greater discipline than many men who called themselves Satyagrahis.
slides.visualDescription: The women of Tamora in the 1930 Jungle Satyagraha — in the Satyagrahi lines, facing the bayonets, being beaten. Their discipline absolute. Their non-retaliation complete. Women as Satyagrahis: not symbolically, not peripherally. As the practice itself, bodily and complete.

slides.text: Dayavati of Tamora — the young Gond woman who stood before the British soldier's rifle and did not move. Her name is known in Tamora. It is known in this series. It is known nowhere else in the national history of the freedom movement. The gap between her courage and her recognition.
slides.visualDescription: Dayavati — the face that deserves a portrait in the national gallery but has none. Her courage: documented locally, ignored nationally. The gap between what she did and what history recorded. This series giving her the frame she was denied. The portrait the gallery forgot.

slides.text: Amar Singh's wife — beaten alongside her husband for refusing to change their slogan. She is not even named in the source material. His name is recorded. Hers is not. She stood before the same lathi, absorbed the same blow, shouted the same name. History recorded only one of them.
slides.visualDescription: Amar Singh's wife in the moment of the Tamora beating — as present, as courageous, as committed as her husband. His name in the record. Hers absent. The woman who stood beside Amar Singh: the most complete proof of history's systematic omission of women's courage.

slides.text: The women of the 1930 Jungle Satyagrahas across Chhattisgarh — Tamora, Nagari-Sihawa, Mahasamund. Women whose names we do not have, whose courage we must infer from the documented fact that they were there. The inference as its own form of historical record.
slides.visualDescription: The women of the Jungle Satyagrahas — undocumented, inferred, present. The documentary gap as itself historical evidence: women were there because movements of this scale do not happen without women. The inference as testimony. The absence in the record as record of systemic erasure.

slides.text: 1933. Gandhi's second visit. The elder woman at the Raipur meeting who asked to wash Gandhi's feet. Her name is not in the record. Her act is — because it moved Gandhi enough that Mahadev Desai recorded it. The act preserved, the actor unnamed.
slides.visualDescription: The elder woman washing Gandhi's feet — her act recorded by Desai, her name lost. The act in the record: the woman bending, washing, drinking the water. The actor: unnamed. History preserving the deed and discarding the doer. The systematic half-memory of women's contributions.

slides.text: The Chamar women of Devri who cooked for Gandhi. Their names are not recorded. Their village is named in the source material. They cooked. He ate. The most intimate act of hospitality — preparing food for a guest — performed by women whose names were not worth recording.
slides.visualDescription: The Devri Chamar women in their kitchen — preparing food for Gandhi. Their hands in the cooking. Their faces as they watch him eat. Their names: unrecorded. Their act: the most intimate hospitality possible. History noting the eating, forgetting the cooking, erasing the cooks.

slides.text: The Baithd School in Durg, founded in 1926 — its integrated classroom where Harijan and upper-caste children sat together. Who founded it? A male principal. Who maintained it daily? The women teachers whose names are not in the source material.
slides.visualDescription: The Baithd School — the principal named, the daily maintenance by women teachers unnamed. The school as a gendered institution: male leadership recorded, female daily work invisible. The school's integration as policy: male. The integration's daily practice: female. The record as gendered architecture.

slides.text: Meera Ben — Madelaine Slade — who traveled with Gandhi throughout the second visit. She is named because she was notable: an Englishwoman, an aristocrat, a disciple. The unnamed Indian women whose lives she shared but whose anonymity she did not share.
slides.visualDescription: Meera Ben named in the record. Beside her: the unnamed Indian women of the movement. The irony: the foreign woman is named, the Indian women unnamed. The record's logic: the exceptional is named; the essential is not. Meera Ben's naming as proof of what it costs to be unnamed.

slides.text: The women who managed the households of imprisoned freedom fighters. Mohammad Yunus went to jail; his seventeen-village zamindari was confiscated. Who managed the family after confiscation? Who fed the children? The unnamed women of the confiscation. Their labor: essential. Their name: absent.
slides.visualDescription: The women who managed after confiscation — Mohammad Yunus in jail, his zamindari gone, the family needing to eat. His wife managing. The children fed somehow. The household surviving the catastrophe of principled male sacrifice. The female labor that made principled male sacrifice possible.

slides.text: Abbas Bhai lost his transport license and his Raipur Bus Service. His family still needed to eat. Someone in his household managed the economy of a family without its primary income. That someone: unnamed. The family of sacrifice, managed in silence by the women of the family.
slides.visualDescription: Abbas Bhai's family after the license cancellation — the household needing to function without the bus service income. The women of the family managing. Unnamed. Essential. Their economic management making Abbas Bhai's sacrifice possible. The invisible economy of principled loss.

slides.text: The lawyers who left their practices in 1920 — Pyarelal Singh, Ramdayal Tiwari. Their wives managed household economies suddenly without professional income. Their wives enabled the sacrifice that history records in their husbands' names. The enablers of the recorded sacrifice.
slides.visualDescription: The wives of the lawyers who left their practices — managing the households that the sacrifice of professional income had disrupted. No income, children to feed, social pressures from families who thought their husbands had lost their minds. The women who said: go. I will manage.

slides.text: The women's participation in the freedom movement was not peripheral. It was structural. The movement ran on the domestic labor of women who managed households while their husbands were in jail, in Satyagraha, in exile, in hiding. No domestic management: no movement.
slides.visualDescription: The structural role of women's domestic labor — visualised as the foundation of the movement. The visible movement (Satyagrahas, meetings, DCC) resting on the invisible foundation (domestic management, child-rearing, household economy). The foundation as essential as the structure.

slides.text: Gandhi understood this. He said it explicitly: women are the backbone of India's freedom movement. He organised women's participation deliberately in every campaign — the Salt March had women marchers, the Non-Cooperation had women boycotters, the Harijan movement had women donors.
slides.visualDescription: Gandhi's deliberate inclusion of women in every campaign — the Salt March women marchers, the women boycotters of foreign cloth, the women donors to the Harijan Fund. Gandhi's understanding that the movement needed women's participation to be genuine. The deliberate inclusion as policy.

slides.text: Gandhi's address to the women's gathering at Machilabad in 1920 — he went specifically to a women's meeting. Not because it was politically strategic, but because he believed women were equal participants in the movement and their meeting deserved his presence equally.
slides.visualDescription: Gandhi at the Machilabad women's gathering — addressing the women directly, specifically, as equals. Not a token appearance. Not a brief greeting. A full meeting. His presence saying: your gathering matters as much as the men's gathering. The message in the attendance itself.

slides.text: The Harijan women who met Gandhi in 1933 — in Devri, in Tamora, in Raipur's Harijan quarter. The women at the intersection of two oppressions: gender and caste. Gandhi meeting them, listening to their particular experience. The double exclusion given double attention.
slides.visualDescription: Gandhi meeting Harijan women in the village circuit — women at the intersection of caste and gender exclusion. Their particular stories: excluded from the temple, excluded from the market, excluded from the school, excluded from the political meeting. Gandhi listening to the specific weight of double exclusion.

slides.text: The Harijan women of Devri who cooked for Gandhi experienced the second visit differently from the men who heard his speeches. For them, Gandhi was not the platform orator — he was the guest who ate their food without hesitation. The Mahatma at their kitchen table.
slides.visualDescription: The Devri women's experience of Gandhi's visit — not the speeches but the meal. Gandhi at their kitchen level. His acceptance of their food as the most radical act he performed in Chhattisgarh. Their experience of this: not as a political event but as a human one. The kitchen as the movement's most essential space.

slides.text: Dayavati is the women's movement of Chhattisgarh in one face. A young Gond woman who stood before a rifle. Whose village was renamed by Gandhi. Whose name is known locally and nowhere else. The complete story of what women gave and what history failed to record.
slides.visualDescription: Dayavati's face as the summary of this episode — the complete story of women's contribution and historical erasure in one face. Her courage: complete. Her recognition: local. Her name: unknown nationally. Gandhigram Tamora: named for Gandhi, not for her. The asymmetry made personal.

slides.text: The women of Chhattisgarh gave their gold to the Tilak Fund in 1920. Stood before bayonets in 1930. Cooked for Gandhi in 1933. Managed households while their husbands were imprisoned. Spun khadi. Organised village meetings. Kept the bricks from the stage. Did half the work. Received none of the record.
slides.visualDescription: The complete accounting of women's contributions — gold given, bayonets faced, food cooked, households managed, khadi spun, meetings organised, bricks kept. Each contribution shown. Then: the record showing none of their names. The gap between contribution and recognition made total.

slides.text: This episode is an act of reparation. Not sufficient — nothing we can do in an episode is sufficient for what was done across decades. But a beginning: naming the category if not always the individual, acknowledging the contribution if not always the contributor.
slides.visualDescription: The episode as reparation — named: the categories of women's contribution. Unnamed still: most of the individual women. The partial reparation as better than nothing. The beginning of an accounting that the official history refused to make. The episode as an act, however insufficient.

slides.text: If Johar Gandhi — the book and this series — has a central failing, it is that the women of the movement remain partially invisible even here. The source material did not name them. The historical record did not keep them. We can only gesture toward the shape of what was erased.
slides.visualDescription: The honest acknowledgement — even this series cannot fully restore what was erased. The women remain partially visible, partially named. The source material's gaps are the series' gaps. The gesture toward the erased shape: the best that can be done with what remains.

slides.text: Future researchers: go to Tamora. Find the descendants of Amar Singh's wife. Find the descendants of the Devri Chamar women. Find the descendants of the Machilabad donors. Their names are there — in living memory, in family stories, in the oral tradition that written history ignored.
slides.visualDescription: The call to future research — Tamora, Devri, Machilabad. The living memory that written history missed. The family stories that carry the names the archive discarded. The oral tradition as the complete archive that the written record refused to be. The future historians as the restorers.

slides.text: Dayavati's name was kept because her act was so extreme that the local memory could not discard it. The rifle, the chest, the not-moving: that image burned itself into Tamora's collective memory and could not be erased. Extremity as the condition of women's historical survival.
slides.visualDescription: Dayavati's name surviving because her act was too extreme to forget — the rifle aimed, the chest forward, the not-moving. Extremity as the condition of survival in the historical record for women. Only the most extreme act was remembered. All else: erased.

slides.text: What does it mean that women had to do something as extreme as standing before a rifle to be remembered? It means the bar for women's historical recognition was set impossibly high. Even so: Dayavati clears it. And behind her: the women who didn't have to stand before a rifle to matter.
slides.visualDescription: Dayavati clearing the impossible bar. Behind her: the unnamed women who also mattered. The bar visible as an unjust structural feature. Dayavati's clearing of it as proof it was possible to be remembered if you did the impossible. The impossibility as the indictment.

slides.text: The women of the movement are half the story of Johar Gandhi. This episode is that half, told in its available form — partial, inferential, often categorical rather than individual. But present. Acknowledged. Counted.
slides.visualDescription: The women of the movement as half the story — this episode as that half. Partial. Inferential. Categorical. But present. The half-told as better than the untold. The acknowledgement as better than the silence. The counting as better than the not-counting. The beginning.

slides.text: The Machilabad women who gave their gold in 1920. The Tamora women who stood before bayonets in 1930. The Devri women who cooked for Gandhi in 1933. The Raipur elder who washed his feet. Four moments. Four types of contribution. One movement. One story. One Chhattisgarh.
slides.visualDescription: Four images in sequence: Machilabad gold, Tamora bayonets, Devri kitchen, Raipur feet-washing. Four moments from 1920, 1930, 1933. Four types of women's contribution. One movement across thirteen years. One Chhattisgarh. Four images as the episode's summary and memorial.

slides.text: Johar: the Chhattisgarhi word of greeting and farewell. It is said to those you respect. This episode says Johar to the women of the Chhattisgarh freedom movement. Named and unnamed. Present in the record and absent from it. Seen by history and unseen by it. Johar.
slides.visualDescription: The word JOHAR directed toward the women of the movement — the named and the unnamed. The word as the greeting they were never given by official history. The series giving it now, belatedly, as an act of retroactive recognition. Johar: to the women who gave everything and got nothing back.

slides.text: One episode remains. The final Johar — the series' farewell to Gandhi, to Chhattisgarh, to the movement, to all who gave everything. The completion of a story that began in 1825 and ended, in some ways, on November 28, 1933, when the train crossed the Chhattisgarh border.
slides.visualDescription: The approach to the final episode — the series gathering its threads. Gandhi and Chhattisgarh. The first martyr and the last farewell. The 1825 beginning and the 1933 ending. The final Johar as the series' most complete act. One episode remaining.

slides.text: Johar to the women. Johar to the unnamed. Johar to Dayavati, to Amar Singh's wife, to the Machilabad donors, to the Devri cooks, to the Raipur elder. Your story is told here. Imperfectly. But told. Next: Episode 10 — Johar.
slides.visualDescription: A final montage of the women of the movement — each face named where possible, unnamed where not. Each contribution acknowledged. The Johar given to each. The series approaching its final episode. Title card: Episode 10 — Johar.
